name: Xerox PARC Ethernet shared cable network
summary: At Xerox PARC by 1974, an experimental Ethernet linked Alto computers and a laser printer over one shared coaxial cable; by 1976 it had 100 nodes.
description: Xerox PARC experimental Ethernet packet network connecting computers over shared coaxial cable.
tier_reason: The scoped record is a particular configuration, local witness, trial or material application. Dependence across fields or generations on THIS referent is not established; do not inherit the importance of its broader missing family.
why: PARC was building many Alto personal computers and a fast laser printer and needed a cheap way for them to share files and printing; ALOHAnet's shared-channel idea was an example.

date.label: by 1974
date.basis: Latest documented event, not a claim to the earliest possible event.

events.statement: By 1974 Xerox PARC used an experimental Ethernet connecting Alto computers and a laser printer.
events.caveats: Metcalfe dates the first experimental network to 1974; IEEE’s retrospective places printer use in 1973. Exact first use is not settled.

evidence.supports: Metcalfe recalls building a network connecting dozens of Altos and a laser printer in 1974.
An IEEE oral-history account says the EARS printer received Alto documents over Ethernet in 1973.
The authors distinguish the distributed DCS ring and central-switching local networks, and credit ALOHA collision/retransmission ideas.

date.label: by 1976-07
date.basis: Latest documented availability or use; no earliest entry date is asserted.

events.statement: The 1976 authors describe an operating Ethernet of 100 nodes along approximately one kilometre of coaxial cable.
events.caveats: The paper does not establish a retail offer or complete adoption by Xerox offices.

evidence.supports: The authors report an operating 100-node system and describe the office and laboratory context.

community_entry.caveats: Metcalfe dates the first experimental network to 1974; IEEE’s retrospective places printer use in 1973. Exact first use is not settled.

links.statement: Ethernet’s developers describe starting its shared-channel design with packet collision and retransmission ideas developed in the ALOHA Network.
links.scope: Specific random-access design ideas, not identity of radio and coaxial implementations.
links.alternatives: Other implementations and technological pathways existed.
links.caveats: Ethernet added carrier sensing and collision detection; this does not say ALOHAnet equipment was installed in the Ethernet.
links.timing: ALOHAnet operational use precedes the 1976 Ethernet paper.

evidence.supports: Metcalfe and Boggs explicitly credit packet collision and retransmission ideas from the ALOHA Network.
